gloss: hair; hairy, the he-goat; barley; bristle, shudder; storm
summary: שֵׂעָר is hair, of the head, the beard and the body; שָׂעִיר, “hairy”, is the shaggy he-goat, the sin offering of every feast and the two goats of the Day of Covering (Lev 16; 23:19), and שְׂעֹרָה is barley, the bristly-eared grain that ripens first (Exo 9:31). The verb is to bristle or shudder with horror, as when “the hair of my flesh stood up” (Job 4:15; Jer 2:12), and once, it seems, to know (Deu 32:17); a few words of the same spelling speak of a storm that whirls away, with no cognate yet tying them to the rest. Arabic šaʿr “hair” and šaʿīr “barley”, Sabaic s²ʿrm “barley”, and Akkadian šārtu “hair” share the root’s main senses.

words.gloss: he-goat, buck (“the hairy one”); goat-idol; wild goat
words.summary: The adjective “hairy” used as a noun: the shaggy he-goat, nearly always “a buck of the goats” (שְׂעִיר עִזִּים) brought for a sin offering. In the plural it is also the goat-shaped idols Israel sacrificed to in the field and Jeroboam set up beside his calves, and the wild goats of desolate ruins. Its uses are counted under BDB’s goat key, which also holds the tokens of the adjective (Gen 27:11, 23) and of the idols.

senses.definition: The male goat brought to Yahweh as a sin offering: by a ruler for his sin, by the congregation, at the new moons and every feast, and on the Day of Covering, when one goat’s blood was brought within the veil and the other, living, bore Israel’s iniquities into the wilderness.

evidence.note: A ruler who has sinned brings “a buck of the goats (שְׂעִיר עִזִּים), a male, whole”: the word names the male of the goats.
At the priests’ consecration Israel brings “a buck of the goats for a sin offering”.
Moses seeks “the goat of the sin offering” and finds it burnt.
“Two bucks of the goats for a sin offering” from the congregation for the Day of Covering.
Lots are cast on the two goats, one for Yahweh and one for עֲזָאזֵל.
He kills the goat of the sin offering for the people and brings its blood within the veil to the covering-lid.
Aaron lays both hands on the head of “the living goat”, confesses over it all Israel’s iniquities, and puts them on its head.
“The goat shall bear (וְנָשָׂא) upon it all their iniquities to a land cut off.”
The bull and goat whose blood was brought into the holy place are burned outside the camp.
At the feast of weeks: “you shall offer one buck of the goats for a sin offering”.
Each prince’s dedication gift includes one buck of the goats for a sin offering (Num 7:16–82).
For the congregation’s unwitting sin.
At the new moons, beside the continual burnt offering.
At the day of shouting, “to make a covering for you”.
Under Hezekiah the goats of the sin offering are brought before the king and the congregation, who lay their hands on them.
“A buck of the goats, whole, for a sin offering”, to purify the altar.

senses.gloss: kid, young he-goat (killed for its blood)
senses.definition: A goat of the flock killed for another purpose: Joseph’s brothers dip his coat in its blood.

evidence.note: “They killed a buck of the goats and dipped the coat in the blood.”

senses.gloss: the shaggy he-goat of Daniel’s vision
senses.definition: In Daniel’s vision the he-goat from the west that breaks the ram is explained as the king of Javan, Greece.

evidence.note: “And the shaggy he-goat (הַצָּפִיר הַשָּׂעִיר) is the king of Javan, and the great horn between its eyes is the first king.”

senses.definition: In the plural, the goats Israel sacrificed to in the open field, and which Jeroboam made and gave priests beside his calves: goat-shaped idols, not living beings.

evidence.note: “They shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to the goats (לַשְּׂעִירִם) after which they go whoring”: the sacrifices made “in the open field” (Lev 17:5) are to be brought to the tent instead.
Jeroboam “appointed priests for the high places, and for the goats and for the calves which he had made”: made things, beside the calves of 1Ki 12:28.

senses.definition: In the plural, goats that roam and leap in a desolate city, named among desert creatures as a sign of its ruin.

evidence.note: In fallen Babylon desert creatures lie down, the houses are full of howling creatures, ostriches dwell, “and שְׂעִירִים shall dance there”.
In desolate Edom desert creatures meet with jackals, “and the שָׂעִיר shall call to his fellow”.

evidence.locator: Lev.16.21 and Lev.23.19, שָׂעִיר → χίμαρος (spelled ξίμαρος in the data); about 30 times in Leviticus and Numbers
evidence.note: Not used in the New Testament.
The shepherd separates the sheep from the goats (ἐρίφων).
“You never gave me a kid (ἔριφον).”
The Greek renders the goat-idols “vain things”.
Paul at Lystra: “that you should turn from these vain things (ματαίων) to the living God”: idols called by the word the Greek gave the שְׂעִירִים.
The Greek’s word where the Hebrew has wild goats dancing in Babylon’s ruins.
Fallen Babylon “has become a habitation of δαιμόνων … and a cage of every unclean bird”: the desolation of Isa 13:21 in the Greek’s words. The Hebrew there is goats.

parallels.note: The calves Jeroboam made, beside the goat-idols.
Desert creatures, with which the goats share the ruins.

phrases.gloss: the goat of the sin offering

words.summary: Barley, the grain with long bristly awns, the first of the grains to ripen: in the ear in Abib when the wheat was not yet up, and harvested from Passover. Mostly plural, שְׂעֹרִים, for the grain as a crop or a measure.

senses.gloss: barley (the crop, the first to ripen)
senses.definition: Barley as a field crop, named with wheat as the staple grains of the land; it ripens before the wheat, and its harvest opens the season.

evidence.note: The hail struck the flax and the barley, “for the barley was in the ear (אָבִיב) and the flax in bud”.
“But the wheat and the spelt were not struck, for they were late.”
“A land of wheat and barley, and vines and figs and pomegranates.”
Naomi and Ruth came to Bethlehem “at the beginning of the barley harvest”.
Ruth gleaned “until the end of the barley harvest and of the wheat harvest”: barley first.
“In the first days, at the beginning of the barley harvest.”
The farmer puts the wheat in rows and the barley in its place.
Farmers wail “for the wheat and for the barley”.
“Let thorns grow instead of wheat, and weeds instead of barley.”

senses.gloss: barley as food, bread and fodder
senses.definition: Barley ground and baked into loaves and cakes, the plain bread of the poor and of soldiers, and fed to horses.

evidence.note: “A loaf of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian”: Gideon, as the dream is read.
A man brings the man of God “bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley”; set before a hundred, they eat and leave some over (2Ki 4:44).
Wheat, barley, beans and lentils in one vessel for siege bread.
“You shall eat it as a barley cake.”
False prophetesses profane Yahweh “for handfuls of barley and for crumbs of bread”.
Barley and straw for the horses.

senses.gloss: barley as a measure and a price
senses.definition: Barley counted by the seah, ephah, homer and lethech, as payment, valuation or offering.

evidence.note: “Two seahs of barley for a shekel in the gate of Samaria.”
Hosea buys his wife back “for fifteen of silver and a homer of barley and a lethech of barley”.
A field is valued by its seed: “a homer of barley seed at fifty shekels of silver”.
The offering of jealousy is a tenth of an ephah of barley meal, with no oil or frankincense.
Ruth beat out about an ephah of barley.

evidence.locator: Rut.1.22; 2Ki.7.1; Hos.3.2, שְׂעֹרָה → κριθή; about 30 times

evidence.note: “Three measures of barley (κριθῆς) for a denarius”: famine prices, as in 2Ki 7:1 the reverse.

evidence.locator: 2Ki.4.42, לֶחֶם שְׂעֹרִים → ἄρτους κριθίνους; Num.5.15; Ezk.4.12

evidence.note: “A lad here has five barley loaves (ἄρτους κριθίνους)”: five thousand fed and twelve baskets left (Jhn 6:13), as Elisha’s twenty barley loaves fed a hundred with some left (2Ki 4:42–44).

parallels.note: Wheat, the grain named with it, and ripening after it.

words.summary: Hair as a mass: of the head, the beard and the whole body, grown or shaved; in the law of skin disease its colour is a sign; and a “garment of hair” is a rough cloak of animal hair, the prophets’ dress.

senses.gloss: hair of the head and body
senses.definition: The hair that grows on a person’s head, beard and body: let grow by the Nazirite, shaved in cleansing and mourning, weighed by Absalom, and praised in the Song.

evidence.note: All the days of his vow no razor comes on the Nazirite’s head; “he shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow”.
At the end he shaves his separated head and puts “the hair of the head of his separation” on the fire under the peace offering.
“The hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.”
Absalom weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king’s weight.
The one being cleansed shaves off all his hair.
“He shall shave all his hair, his head and his beard and his eyebrows, all his hair he shall shave.”
Ezra plucked out “the hair of my head and of my beard” in grief.
Yahweh will shave with the razor hired beyond the River, the king of Assyria, “the head and the hair of the feet”.
Jerusalem pictured as a girl grown up: “your hair had grown”.
“Your hair is like a flock of goats that leap down from Mount Gilead”: the hair likened to goats.
God strikes “the hairy crown (קָדְקֹד שֵׂעָר) of him who goes on in his guilt”.

senses.gloss: hair in a skin disease (as a sign)
senses.definition: In the law of צָרַעַת the hair in a diseased patch shows the priest its state: hair turned white or thin yellow hair marks it unclean, and black hair grown in it shows it healed.

evidence.note: “If the hair in the plague has turned white … it is a plague of צָרַעַת.”
Thin yellow hair in a scall of the head or beard.
“If black hair has grown in it, the scall is healed; he is clean.”

senses.definition: Hair worked into a rough cloak, the dress of the prophets; Esau at birth was “like a garment of hair” all over.

evidence.note: “The first came out red, all of him like a garment of hair (כְּאַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר), and they called his name Esau.”
Elijah is known as “a man, a possessor of hair (בַּעַל שֵׂעָר), with a girdle of leather bound about his loins”.
In that day the prophets will be ashamed “and will not wear a garment of hair (אַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר) to deceive”.
John “had his garment of camel’s hair and a girdle of leather about his loins”: Elijah’s dress (Mat 11:14).

evidence.locator: Lev.13.3; Num.6.5; Jdg.16.22, שֵׂעָר → θρίξ; about 20 times; also שַׂעֲרָה (Jdg.20.16; 1Sa.14.45; 1Ki.1.52)

evidence.note: John’s garment ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλου, of camel’s hair.
“You cannot make one hair white or black.”
“The very hairs of your head are all numbered.”
“Not a hair of your head shall perish”, the oath of 1Sa 14:45 made a promise.
“Not a hair shall fall from the head of any of you”, in the words of 1Sa 14:45 and 1Ki 1:52.
She wiped his feet with the hairs of her head.
“His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow”, as the Ancient of Days in Dan 7:9.

phrases.gloss: a possessor of hair, a man in a hair garment

words.gloss: bristle, shudder; (once) know; storm, sweep away
words.summary: A rare verb of eight uses whose senses fall in three groups. In the qal it is to shudder, bristle with horror, beside “be appalled” (Jer 2:12; Ezk 27:35; 32:10), the hair standing as in Job 4:15; once, set parallel to “know”, it seems to be “know, be acquainted with” (Deu 32:17), as in Sabaic and Arabic. In Psa 58:10 and the niphal, piel and hithpael it is to storm, to whirl away as a tempest: no cognate yet ties this group to the root, and it may be a second older root of the same spelling, near Hebrew סער “storm”.

stems.gloss: shudder, bristle with horror; know (?); sweep away

senses.definition: Be seized with horror at a calamity, set beside being appalled and trembling; used with its own noun, “shudder a shuddering”.

evidence.note: “Be appalled (שֹׁמּוּ), O heavens, at this, and shudder (וְשַׂעֲרוּ), be very desolate”, at Israel forsaking the fountain of living waters.
Over fallen Tyre the coastlands are appalled, “and their kings shudder a shuddering (שָׂעֲרוּ שַׂעַר), their faces are troubled”.
Over Pharaoh “their kings shall shudder a shuddering … and they shall tremble (וְחָרְדוּ) every moment”.

senses.definition: In its one use with an object, set parallel to “know”: the new gods Israel sacrificed to were ones “whom your fathers did not שׂער”. Sabaic and Arabic both use the root for knowing and being aware; the sense “shudder at, dread” is also possible here.

evidence.note: “They sacrificed to שֵׁדִים, not God, gods whom they did not know (לֹא יְדָעוּם), new ones come lately, whom your fathers did not שְׂעָרוּם.”

senses.definition: Carry off suddenly, as a whirlwind sweeps away the thorns before the pot feels their heat.

evidence.note: “Before your pots feel the thorns, green or burning, he will sweep it away (יִשְׂעָרֶנּוּ).”

stems.gloss: be stormy, rage as a storm

senses.definition: Of the tempest about God as he comes to judge.

evidence.note: “Our God comes and does not keep silent; fire devours before him, and round about him it storms (נִשְׂעֲרָה) greatly.”

senses.definition: Of the east wind carrying a wicked man off from his place.

evidence.note: “The east wind lifts him up and he is gone, and it whirls him away (וִישָׂעֲרֵהוּ) from his place.”

senses.gloss: storm against, rush upon like a whirlwind
senses.definition: Of a king coming against another with overwhelming force.

evidence.note: “At the time of the end the king of the south shall push at him, and the king of the north shall storm against him (וְיִשְׂתָּעֵר עָלָיו) with chariots and horsemen and many ships, and shall overflow and pass through.”

evidence.locator: Jer.2.12, וְשַׂעֲרוּ → ἔφριξεν (spelled ἔφριχεν in the data)

evidence.note: “The demons also believe, and shudder (φρίσσουσιν).”

parallels.note: “Know”, in the parallel line of Deu 32:17.
The east wind that carries off, beside the whirling away.

words.summary: One hair, the smallest thing: what a slinger can hit, what may not fall from a man’s head if he is to be kept safe, and, in the plural, what is too many to count.

senses.gloss: a hair; not a hair (of complete safety)
senses.definition: A single hair, as the least thing: a mark too fine to miss for a skilled slinger, and in the oath “not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground”, the promise that a man will come to no harm at all.

evidence.note: Seven hundred left-handed men of Benjamin “could sling a stone at a hair and not miss”.
“As Yahweh lives, not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day”; so the people redeemed Jonathan and he did not die.
David to the woman of Tekoa: “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”
Solomon of Adonijah: “If he is a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth.”
“Not a hair of your head shall perish.”

senses.gloss: hairs of the head (as past counting)
senses.definition: In the plural, the hairs of the head as a number past counting: the psalmist’s iniquities and enemies are more than they.

evidence.note: “Evils without number have surrounded me … they are more than the hairs of my head.”
“Those who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head.”
What man cannot count, God has: “the very hairs of your head are all numbered”.

senses.gloss: hair of the flesh (standing on end)
senses.definition: The hair of the body bristling with dread: the bodily sense behind the verb “shudder”.

evidence.note: “A spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh (שַׂעֲרַת בְּשָׂרִי) stood up (תְּסַמֵּר).”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, as Hebrew שֵׂעָר: the hair of the head, three times in Daniel.

senses.definition: The hair of a man’s head, or of the Ancient of Days in Daniel’s vision.

evidence.note: The fire had no power on their bodies, “and the hair of their head was not singed”.
Nebuchadnezzar driven out “until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers”.
The Ancient of Days sat; “his garment white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool”.
The one like a son of man: “his head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow”.

words.summary: Four uses: three of the shuddering of horror, the noun of the qal verb, and one of a storm. Whether the storm (Isa 28:2) is the same word or a second root of the same spelling is not clear; no cognate yet ties the storm sense to the root.

senses.definition: The shudder of horror that seizes those who see a great fall.

evidence.note: At the wicked man’s day “those who come after are appalled (נָשַׁמּוּ), and those who went before seize horror (שַׂעַר)”.
“Their kings shudder a shuddering.”

senses.definition: A destroying tempest, set beside a storm of hail and overflowing waters.

evidence.note: The Lord’s mighty one comes “like a downpour of hail, a storm of destruction (שַׂעַר קָטֶב), like a downpour of mighty overflowing waters”.

words.summary: The feminine of שָׂעִיר: a female goat, brought by one of the people for a sin offering.

senses.definition: A female of the goats, whole, which one of the common people brings for his sin, where a ruler brings a male.

evidence.note: “He shall bring his offering, a she-goat of the goats (שְׂעִירַת עִזִּים), whole, a female, for his sin.”
“A female from the flock, a lamb or a she-goat of the goats, for a sin offering, and the priest shall make a covering for him.”

evidence.locator: Lev.4.28; Lev.5.6, שְׂעִירַת → χίμαιραν (spelled ξίμαιραν in the data)
evidence.note: Not used in the New Testament.

words.summary: Hairy, of Esau’s body against Jacob’s smooth skin. It is the same word as שָׂעִיר, spelled without the yod, and BDB counts its two uses under the goat’s key, so it carries no key of its own here; Jacob’s hands were made hairy with the skins of kids of the goats (Gen 27:16).

senses.definition: Covered with hair, of a man’s body.

evidence.note: “Esau my brother is a hairy man (אִישׁ שָׂעִר), and I am a smooth man (אִישׁ חָלָק).”
Isaac did not know him, “because his hands were hairy (שְׂעִרֹת), like the hands of Esau his brother”.
Rebekah put the skins of the kids of the goats on his hands and neck.
Not used in the New Testament.

words.summary: A storm wind, twice, of Yahweh’s way and of his crushing of Job. Like the verb’s storm senses, it has no cognate yet tying it to the root, and stands close to Hebrew סְעָרָה “storm”, of another root key.

senses.definition: A violent wind, in which Yahweh goes and by which he can crush.

evidence.note: “Yahweh: in the whirlwind (בְּסוּפָה) and in the storm (וּבִשְׂעָרָה) is his way, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.”
“He who would crush me with a tempest and multiply my wounds without cause.”

words.summary: Once, in the plural, of rain on the grass, beside dew and showers. How it comes from the root is not clear: it has the form of the plural of שָׂעִיר, but no verse or cognate shows why rain would be called so.

senses.definition: Fine rain falling on young grass, one of four images for Moses’ teaching.

evidence.note: “Let my teaching drop as the rain (כַּמָּטָר), my speech distil as the dew, as שְׂעִירִם on the tender grass, and as showers (וְכִרְבִיבִים) on the herb.”
“When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, A shower (ὄμβρος) is coming.”

parallels.note: “Rain”, the first of the verse’s four images.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܣܥܪܐ (saʿrā), hair, for Greek θρίξ: the same word as Hebrew שֵׂעָר, with Syriac s for Hebrew ś.

senses.definition: The hair of the head, of a garment of hair, and of the son of man in John’s vision.

evidence.note: John’s clothing was “of camel’s hair”.
“You cannot make one hair white or black.”
She wiped his feet with the hair of her head.
“If a man has long hair, it is a dishonour to him.”
“His head and his hair were white like wool, and like snow.”
The sun became black “like sackcloth of hair”.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܣܥܪܐ (sʿārā), barley, as Hebrew שְׂעֹרָה; in the plural for John’s barley loaves, and in Paul’s seed that is sown as “bare grain of wheat or of barley”.

senses.definition: Barley as bread, as a price, and as seed that is sown and rises in another body.

evidence.note: “A boy here has five loaves of barley and two fish.”
“Three measures of barley for a denarius.”
The Peshitta reads “a bare grain of wheat or of barley”, where the Greek has “or of some other grain”.

cognates.gloss: hair (of men and animals); a single hair
cognates.note: Lane’s sources define it as hair “that grows upon the body, that is not wool nor camel’s fur”, of human beings and other animals, used for goats’ hair when spoken of tent-cloth; the noun of unity šaʿra is one hair, as Hebrew שַׂעֲרָה. Arabic ʿ (ع), not ġ (غ), stands behind ע.

evidence.note: “Hair; i. e. what grows upon the body, that is not صُوف nor وَبَر … an appertenance of human beings and of other animals … the n. un. is with ة.”

evidence.locator: SEM000469 śʿr [hair] N: ARB015709 šaʿr; ARM021333 sʿr; GEZ005305 śəʿərt; HEB007623 śeʿar; UGC003950 šʿr

cognates.gloss: hairy, having much hair; (of a goat) shaggy
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give ʾašʿar and šaʿir of a man having much hair on his body, and “the first and second, a goat having much hair”: the adjective, and its use for a shaggy goat, as Hebrew שָׂעִיר.

evidence.note: “A man having much hair upon his body … and the first and second, a goat having much hair.”

cognates.gloss: barley; n. un. šaʿīra a barleycorn
cognates.note: The same pattern of the same root as the word for hair, as Hebrew שְׂעֹרָה beside שֵׂעָר.

evidence.note: “Barley; a certain grain, well known … n. un. with ة [signifying a barleycorn].”

cognates.gloss: know, perceive, be aware of; knowledge
cognates.note: The verb of knowing and perceiving, whose noun also gives “poetry”. It answers to the qal of Deu 32:17, set parallel to יָדַע.

evidence.note: “He knew it; knew, or had knowledge, of it; was cognizant of it; or understood it … or he perceived it by means of [any of] the senses.”
“Knowledge; cognizance … لَيْتَ شِعْرِى … Would that I knew.”

cognates.gloss: (of the skin) quake, shudder; a shudder of the skin
cognates.note: A four-letter root qšʿr whose last three letters are this root; “said of the skin, it quaked, shuddered”, which is what the hair standing up of Job 4:15 and the shuddering of Jer 2:12 describe. Whether the q is a prefix to šʿr is not shown, so it is marked possible.

evidence.note: “Said of the skin, It quaked; shuddered; was, or became, affected by a tremor … A tremor, quaking, or quivering, of the skin seized him.”

cognates.gloss: (Sabaic) know, be aware/conscious of; n. knowledge
cognates.note: Sabaic pairs it with the verb “know” just as Deu 32:17 pairs שׂער with יָדַע: C 429/7 “of whom they did not know and were not aware (s²ʿrw)”. Sabaic s² answers to Hebrew שׂ.

evidence.note: “KNOW, BE AWARE/CONSCIOUS OF [cf. Ar šaʿara id.] C429/7: … ‘of whom they did not know and were not aware’; C532/8–9: she committed sins ‘those of which she was conscious, and those she was not aware of’.” Read from the OCR text layer.

cognates.note: Named with wheat, as in Deu 8:8: “crops and harvests (of) sqy-crops, wheat and barley”.

evidence.note: “BARLEY [cf. Ar šaʿīr id.] J670/26–7: may the god grant them … ‘crops and harvests (of) sqy-crops, wheat and barley’.” Read from the OCR text layer.

cognates.note: Akkadian has lost the ʿ, as it usually does, and keeps š for older ś. Over three hundred uses across the periods, of hair and wool.

evidence.locator: armep x000002700, šārtu [hair] N: hair; wool (×335)

cognates.note: The doubled-stem adjective of the same root: the hairy man, as Esau is אִישׁ שָׂעִר.

evidence.locator: armep x000034670, šuʾʾuru [hairy] AJ: unshorn (Middle Assyrian); armep x000075510, šuʾʾuru [hairy one] N: unshaven one (Old Babylonian)

cognates.note: Animal hair as wool, in an administrative text.

evidence.note: “šʿrt 4.630:7 … ‘wool’ (cf. Akkad. šartu, H. śēʿār, Arab. šaʿ(a)r ‘hair’).” Read from the OCR text layer, which garbles the transliteration.

doctrine.statement: A goat for a sin offering was brought at every new moon and feast, at the feast of weeks “one buck of the goats for a sin offering” (Lev 23:19; Num 28:15, 22, 30; 29:5). On the Day of Covering there were two: one killed, its blood brought within the veil to the covering-lid and its body burned outside the camp (Lev 16:15, 27); on the other, living, Aaron laid both hands and confessed all Israel’s iniquities, and “the goat shall bear (נָשָׂא) upon it all their iniquities to a land cut off” (Lev 16:21–22). Isaiah says of the servant, “Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all … he bore (נָשָׂא) the sin of many” (Isa 53:6, 12); Hebrews, that Christ entered the holy place “not by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood” (Heb 9:12), since “it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins” (Heb 10:4), and that as the bodies of the beasts whose blood was brought into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp, “Jesus also … suffered outside the gate” (Heb 13:11–12); he “was offered once to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28), and “bore our sins in his own body on the tree” (1Pe 2:24). From the verses: the two goats showed in two acts what the one offering does, sin dealt with by a death whose blood is brought before God, and sin carried away so that it is gone; the goats could only show it, and Christ did it.

The שְׂעִירִים Israel sacrificed to were things in the open field “after which they go whoring”, and the law brought those sacrifices to the tent of meeting instead (Lev 17:5–7); Jeroboam “appointed priests for the high places, and for the goats and for the calves which he had made” (2Ch 11:15), made things like the calves of Bethel and Dan (1Ki 12:28); and in Isaiah the שְׂעִירִים are animals dancing and calling among the ostriches and desert creatures of a ruined city (Isa 13:21; 34:14). Moses calls the new gods Israel sacrificed to “not God”, ones “your fathers did not know” (Deu 32:17, 21). Paul, quoting that verse, first asks, “What do I say then? that an idol is anything, or that what is offered to idols is anything?” (1Co 10:19–20), having said “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one” (1Co 8:4); and at Lystra he calls the gods men sacrificed to “these vain things” (Act 14:15), the Greek’s own word for the שְׂעִירִים of Lev 17:7. From the verses: the goat-gods were images men made and wild beasts of the waste; the sin was in turning from Yahweh to them, not in any power they had, for there is none other God.

Barley ripens first: when the hail fell in Egypt “the barley was in the ear (אָבִיב)” while “the wheat and the spelt were not struck, for they were late” (Exo 9:31–32), and Abib is the month of the Passover (Exo 13:4); the barley harvest begins at that season and the wheat follows (Rut 1:22; 2:23; 2Sa 21:9). So the sheaf of “the firstfruits of your harvest”, waved before Yahweh “on the morrow after the sabbath” of the feast of unleavened bread (Lev 23:10–11), was of the barley, and the wheat was offered fifty days later at the feast of weeks (Exo 34:22; Lev 23:15–17). Paul writes, “now is Christ risen from the dead, the firstfruits of them that slept … Christ the firstfruits, afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming” (1Co 15:20, 23), and Christ rose on the first day of the week after the sabbath (Mat 28:1); in the same chapter the Peshitta’s seed that is sown and given a new body is “a bare grain of wheat or of barley” (1Co 15:37). From the verses: the first of the barley, offered on the day after the sabbath, set out Christ raised as the first of the harvest of the dead, with the rest of the harvest to follow at his coming.

“Not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground” is Israel’s oath that a man will come to no harm at all: so the people swore for Jonathan, and he did not die (1Sa 14:45), and David for the widow’s son (2Sa 14:11). The hairs of the head are the psalmist’s measure of what is past counting (Psa 40:13; 69:5). Jesus says “the very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Mat 10:30; Luk 12:7), and, of those to be betrayed and some put to death for his name, “not a hair of your head shall perish; in your endurance you will gain your souls” (Luk 21:16–19); Paul in the storm uses Israel’s words, “not a hair shall fall from the head of any of you”, and all came safe to land (Act 27:34, 44). From the verses: God counts what man cannot, and his promise that not a hair will perish is the oath’s full safety given to his disciples, even where it means life kept through death.

In Daniel’s vision the Ancient of Days sits with “the hair of his head like pure wool” (Dan 7:9), and one like a son of man is brought to him and given dominion (Dan 7:13–14). In John’s vision the one like a son of man has “his head and his hairs white like wool, as white as snow” (Rev 1:13–14): the son of man bears the look Daniel gave the Ancient of Days. Jesus says “he who has seen me has seen the Father” (Jhn 14:9), and Hebrews calls the Son “the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3). From the verses: the Son who comes to the Ancient of Days is shown in the Father’s own likeness, God’s glory made known in him.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Leviticus 23 (שְׂעִיר עִזִּים, Lev 23:19) and Numbers 10. Root key שׂער as the database keys it. BDB keys: the goat key u.bs.ag shares all 59 tokens with u.bs.af (adjective “hairy”) and u.bs.aj (“satyr, demon”), so only u.bs.ag is named; the adjective שָׂעִר (Gen 27:11, 23) is kept as its own word with no key, and the goat-idols of Lev 17:7; 2Ch 11:15 and wild goats of Isa 13:21; 34:14 are senses of שָׂעִיר, not a word of their own. The verb’s three BDB keys (u.bs.ad “bristle”, u.bt.aa “sweep away”, u.bu.aa “be acquainted with”) share the same eight tokens, so one verb is entered under u.bs.ad; likewise the noun שַׂעַר under u.bs.ae (u.bt.ab shares its four tokens). Left out as proper names: שֵׂעִיר Seir (u.bs.am; the land of Esau, a mountain in Judah, and Seir the Horite, Seir@Gen.36.20), שְׂעִירָה Seirah (u.bs.ai, a place), שְׂעֹרִים Seorim (u.bs.al, a priest, Seorim@1Ch.24.8), and v.eu.ad (zero tokens). Gen 25:25 ties Esau to hair and Gen 36:8 sets him in Seir; a name entry for Seir the Horite, if wanted, would link here. Not entered: Hebrew סער “storm” (סַעַר, סְעָרָה), a separate root key, which the storm words here stand close to; Coptic ⲥⲟⲣⲧ “wool” (Egyptian, not Semitic and not a loan); Syriac ܣܥܪ “visit, do” (SEDRA root 1298), which answers to Jewish Aramaic סְעַר “visit” and not to this root. Peshitta: SEDRA root 1299 SER, lexemes 2176 ܣܥܪܐ “hair” and 2177 ܣܥܪܐ “barley”, verses found through the BFBS word list (Mat 10:30 and Luk 21:18 use another Syriac word). Not consulted: Dillmann and Leslau for the Geʿez (cited from Anderson–Moser only), DULAT for the Ugaritic (Segert’s glossary read only from OCR, transliterations garbled), Payne Smith for the Syriac senses. Open questions: (1) whether the storm group (the verb’s Psa 58:10, niphal, piel, hithpael; שַׂעַר Isa 28:2; שְׂעָרָה) is a second older root; no cognate supports it either way; (2) Deu 32:17 read as “know” on the Sabaic and Arabic evidence and the parallel יָדַע, against “shudder at”; (3) שְׂעִירִים “showers” (Deu 32:2) kept with no understood link; (4) the barley-firstfruits doctrine infers the grain of Lev 23:10 from the order of ripening, since Lev 23 does not name it; (5) the δαιμόνιον rendering of Isa 13:21 and Rev 18:2 recorded with a note that the Hebrew is goats; (6) לַעֲזָאזֵל (Lev 16:8, 10, 26) is left to its own entry.
